Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
Marcus Calloway is a 58-year-old dentist who has practiced in a mid-sized Ohio city for nearly three decades. He is in a long-term relationship and, until roughly fourteen months ago, was regarded by colleagues and patients alike as steady, meticulous, and warm. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 77, seeking help for the first time after what he describes as a year of "trying to hold the walls up by myself."

The event that fractured his life occurred on a Saturday evening when Marcus was returning from a continuing-education conference. He had parked several blocks from a restaurant where he was meeting his partner for dinner and was walking alone along a well-lit commercial street when two uniformed officers stopped him without explanation, ordered him to the ground, and, when he asked why, struck him repeatedly - first with an open hand, then with a baton across his lower back and left thigh. He was handcuffed and held face-down on the pavement for nearly twenty minutes before being released without charge or apology. No complaint he subsequently filed produced any documented response. The officers were never identified by name in any official record. Marcus drove himself home that night, did not go to the emergency room, and told his partner only that he had been "roughed up." He returned to his practice the following Monday.

In the weeks after, the memory did not behave like other memories. Marcus describes it as something that seems to have happened to a stranger whose body he is merely borrowing - a dissociative quality that disturbs him precisely because he knows it was him on that pavement. Yet the estrangement offers no protection: when the memory surfaces, he hears the specific crack of the baton on concrete and the officer's voice saying "stay down," and he feels a dull, insistent ache radiating from his lower back into his left thigh - the same geography of pain from that night - as though the tissue itself remembers what his mind tries to hold at arm's length.

His dental practice has become one of the primary arenas in which his changed relationship to the world is visible. Each morning he arrives early enough to claim the chair at the far corner of the waiting room - his back to the wall, sight lines to both the entrance and the hallway - before any patients arrive. In the operatory he works with the door slightly ajar, and when a new patient enters he finds himself cataloguing them: their size, how they hold their hands, whether they make eye contact. He had come to believe, with a conviction he cannot fully articulate, that something particular about him had invited what happened - something in how he carries himself, or perhaps something more essential and unnameable - and this belief has made every unfamiliar person who approaches his chair feel like a potential confirmation of that assessment. A pharmaceutical representative who came to the office unannounced last spring sent Marcus into a prolonged state of vigilance that his receptionist noticed and quietly mentioned to the office manager.

Outside work, Marcus has progressively narrowed his life. He and his partner used to attend jazz concerts, a shared pleasure that involved crowds, low lighting, and unpredictable sound - conditions that now feel intolerable. He has declined every invitation that might carry emotional weight in either direction, avoiding not only situations that could frighten him but also celebrations, dinners with close friends, moments that might require him to feel something fully. His partner has absorbed this contraction with patience that is, by Marcus's own account, beginning to fray. They have not been to a restaurant together in eight months.

What Marcus returns to, again and again in early sessions, is the absence of any accountability. He is certain that what was done to him was a profound injustice and that the institutional silence surrounding it has compounded the original harm in ways he cannot measure. He does not believe his life will ever resemble what it was. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when he caught himself choosing a parking space not by proximity to his destination but by how many exits the surrounding block offered. Standing in the lot, keys in hand, he recognised that he had reorganised his entire existence around a threat that never announced itself before it arrived - and that he was exhausted by the vigilance of trying to see it coming.
